oneliner.t: Republican from Calhoun County who has represented east Alabama's 3rd District since 2003 and chairs the House Armed Services Committee; a former county commissioner and state House minority leader, he won the May 19, 2026 GOP primary and faces Democrat Lee McInnis.

hometown.t: Blue Mountain / Saks area, Calhoun County, Alabama (family left Calhoun County in 1957 for work and returned in 1967)

upbringing.t: Rogers was born in Hammond, Indiana, after his family left Calhoun County to find work; they returned in 1967. His father, Clyde Rogers, was a firefighter at Anniston Army Depot, and his mother, Linda Perryman Rogers, worked at a textile mill (Classe Ribbon Company); his official bio says he grew up in the Blue Mountain mill village. He graduated from Saks High School, earned a political science degree (1981) and an MPA (1984) at Jacksonville State University, and a law degree with honors from Birmingham School of Law (1991), the same year as his wife, Beth. He then opened a law practice in Anniston. He married Beth Phillips, now a Calhoun County district judge, in 1982; they have three children.

career.role: Calhoun County Commissioner (youngest ever; first Republican)
State Representative, District 36 (minority leader from his second term)
U.S. Representative, AL-3; Armed Services ranking member 2021–2023, chairman 2023–present; Homeland Security ranking member 2019–2021

platform.t: Says he works to fund the military, resource warfighters and deter China and other adversaries; promotes Anniston Army Depot ('Pit Crew of America's Warfighters').
Takes credit for initiating and overseeing creation of the U.S. Space Force.
Co-sponsored the Sanctity of Human Life Act; his office publicized support for anti-abortion legislation during the January 2026 March for Life.
Office announced support for pro-law-enforcement measures during National Police Week (May 2026).
Introduced bills (American Sovereignty Act of 2017; H.R. 204 in 2019) to withdraw the U.S. from the UN; neither was enacted.

claims.claim: Chairman of the House Armed Services Committee.

said.where: official House bio (mikerogers.house.gov/about) — campaign site unreachable

record.t: He became chairman in January 2023 and led the House side of the FY2026 NDAA, enacted Dec. 18, 2025 (P.L. 119-60).

claims.claim: Was Ranking Member of the Homeland Security Committee in the 116th Congress.

record.t: Ranking member of House Homeland Security 2019–2021.

claims.claim: Initiated and oversaw the creation of the U.S. Space Force, with bipartisan support.

record.t: With Rep. Jim Cooper (D) he proposed a Space Corps in 2017; it passed the House but died in the Senate. Similar language was later enacted to create the Space Force (FY2020 NDAA). He was a lead originator, but enactment also required the Senate and the administration.

claims.claim: Holds a political science degree and an MPA from Jacksonville State and graduated with honors from Birmingham School of Law.

record.t: B.A. 1981, MPA 1984 (JSU); law degree with honors, 1991.

claims.claim: Married to Beth for over 40 years; father of three.

record.t: Married Beth Phillips in 1982; three children.

claims.claim: Mother worked in the local textile mill; father was a firefighter.

record.t: Father Clyde Rogers was a firefighter at Anniston Army Depot; mother Linda Perryman Rogers was a textile worker at Classe Ribbon Company.
Beat Democrat Joe Turnham Jr. 50%–48% in 2002.

claims.claim: Was a practicing attorney and small business owner in Calhoun County.

record.t: Opened his own law firm in Anniston after earning his law degree in 1991 — a small business in Calhoun County.
Repeated by Wikipedia, apparently from his own biography; no independent genealogy found.

entries.t: Voted Yea on the Fiscal Responsibility Act (debt-limit suspension with spending caps).
Voted Yea on H.R. 1 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act), which included a $5 trillion debt-limit increase.
Urged the White House to approve a missile system for Ukraine 'without delay' (per 1819 News headline).
Voted Yea on H.R. 8035, the Ukraine Security Supplemental.
As Armed Services chairman, voted Yea on the final FY2026 NDAA agreement (S. 1071), which passed 312–112.

note.t: LegiStorm's index of his House filings lists annual reports every year 2003–2026 (extension letters in 2021 and 2022) and no periodic transaction (stock-trade) reports for the member; PTRs listed there belong to a former staffer. The PDFs themselves could not be located on the Clerk's site, so no net-worth range or asset list is recorded. His leadership PAC is American Security PAC (C00439521).

effectiveness.note: Sponsored/enacted bill counts not available: congress.gov blocked and his House site's sponsored-bills list did not render. As chairman he led the House side of the FY2026 NDAA (enacted as S. 1071, P.L. 119-60, Dec. 18, 2025).

democracy.t: Signed the House Republicans' December 2020 amicus brief backing Texas v. Pennsylvania, which sought to overturn results in four states; the Supreme Court declined the case.
Voted Yea on the objection to Arizona's electoral votes (failed 121–303).
Voted Yea on the objection to Pennsylvania's electoral votes (failed 138–282).
Was at the Capitol during the attack; the next day tweeted that 'there is no place for political violence in America.'

townhalls.note: A constituent town hall in 2017 is documented (Wikipedia); his House site offers telephone town-hall sign-up. No 2025–2026 in-person town hall or debate was found. His challenger says voters have lacked chances to meet him for about a decade; Rogers did not respond to WTVM.

note.t: Born in Indiana in 1958; family returned to Calhoun County in 1967. Lives in the district.

checks.legal: Courts: CourtListener blocked (known limit); Justia and Alacourt not searched. Reviewed Wikipedia and Encyclopedia of Alabama: no criminal or civil case against Rogers. A constituent filed a complaint with Oxford police over Rogers' remarks at a 2017 town hall ('be a man or we'll take it outside'); no charge is reported. Ethics: House Ethics and Office of Congressional Conduct sites were not fetched; secondary sources report no ethics finding.
checks.foreign: No House financial-disclosure PDF could be opened (Clerk search form not automatable; PDF IDs not found by search). FARA database blocked (known limit). News sources reviewed show no foreign-government or foreign-business tie.
checks.claims: Mechanical sample: the campaign site (mikerogersforcongress.com) could not be fetched, so the official House bio page (mikerogers.house.gov/about) was used — every checkable claim on it (9 rated). No issues page or ads were reachable or found in news coverage (he faced only a minor primary challenger).
checks.democracy: Clerk roll calls 10 and 11 of 2021 read directly; Ballotpedia and Wikipedia for the Texas v. Pennsylvania amicus and Jan. 2021 statements. No statement on 2024 results found.

recordx.note: Disclosure timeliness inferred from LegiStorm's index: no extension letters for 2023–2026 annual reports (extensions in 2021 and 2022). FEC: no RFAIs/notices shown on the committee or candidate pages for 2023–2026. missed_pct not available (GovTrack blocked).

corp.t: His House campaign took $721,704.50 from non-party committees (PACs) in 2025–26 and $7.93M (43.5%) of $18.24M raised across the 11 cycles retrieved (2004–2014, 2018–2026); a business-vs-ideological split isn't available. 1819 News, citing OpenSecrets, reported Lockheed Martin-affiliated individuals and its PAC were his largest contributor in the 2022 cycle ($60,750) while it competed for a missile-defense contract (Next Generation Interceptor) he urged be accelerated; it reported the same for a Ukraine missile system in Jan. 2023.

lobby.t: Track AIPAC lists $1,033,286 in career donations from pro-Israel PACs (AIPAC, NORPAC and nine others) and their large donors; $0 in pro-Israel independent expenditures.

research_notes: MONEY: 2026-cycle figures are from the FEC candidate page (principal committee C00367862, thru 2026-06-30). 'other' = $2,891.29 in transfers from authorized committees + $38,524.99 other receipts. The committee refunded $15,000 to other committees and transferred $132,125.86 to other authorized committees. Career figures sum the FEC committee summaries for 2004–2014 and 2018–2026; the 2002 and 2016 pages hit FEC rate limits and were not retried. Track AIPAC's $1,033,286 is a career figure that includes individual donations from pro-Israel PAC donors, not only PAC checks. No outside spending for or against him in 2026 was found. PROFILE: residence differs by source — Wikipedia says Weaver, Encyclopedia of Alabama says Saks. Wikipedia also reports a January 2023 floor confrontation with Rep. Matt Gaetz during the Speaker vote and that he called opponents of McCarthy 'legislative terrorists'; not used as a claim. Photo not retrieved (Wikimedia not fetched).
